checkpoints: A `Set<string>` that records every clickId ever seen and is never evicted grows monotonically with total traffic, so under billions of clicks per day the process eventually exhausts memory and OOMs — this is a data-structure-shape problem, not a leak in the counting logic itself.

Because that same `seen` set lives only in process memory, any restart (deploy, crash, rebalance) wipes it clean, so a clickId that Kafka redelivers after the restart looks brand-new to the consumer and gets counted a second time, silently inflating ad-click totals.

These are two independent failures with two independent root causes — unbounded growth causes the OOM, loss of in-memory state on restart causes the recount — and conflating them into one fix (e.g. just periodically clearing the set) solves neither properly.

Bounding memory only requires catching duplicates that arrive within the realistic redelivery/retry window, not remembering a clickId forever, so scoping dedup to a TTL turns an ever-growing set into a structure whose size is capped by window length times throughput.

`SET clickId 1 NX EX <ttlSeconds>` in Redis makes the has-it-been-seen check and the mark-it-as-seen write a single atomic round-trip, which is what `NX` buys over a plain get-then-set; a compacted RocksDB column family is the local alternative when a network hop per event is too costly.

Moving the dedup index into an external, durable store (Redis or a replicated/persisted RocksDB) makes it survive process restarts, since a redelivered clickId is still found and correctly rejected instead of looking new — this is what actually fixes the recount bug, separately from the TTL fix for memory.

Kafka transactional producers with `read_committed` consumers give true exactly-once delivery and would eliminate the dedup problem entirely, but that comes at real throughput and operational-complexity cost compared to a TTL-based external store.

A TTL-based fix trades one failure mode for a narrower one: a duplicate that arrives after the window has expired is no longer recognized and gets re-counted, so the window must be sized to the slowest realistic retry rather than the median, and an external store adds a network round-trip to every `record()` call — so validating the fix means confirming memory stays flat over hours, a post-restart redelivery is still rejected, and p99 latency hasn't just moved the cost from memory into the network hop.
